opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the hardest and most fascinating problems in biology, and it's something we think about a lot as we move beyond AlphaFold toward the bigger dream of a virtual cell.

The issue is that cellular processes span an enormous range of scales. At the bottom you have atomic vibrations and bond rotations happening in femtoseconds. Then protein folding and conformational changes in microseconds to milliseconds. Then signaling cascades and metabolic fluxes over seconds to minutes. Then gene expression, cell division and differentiation over hours or days. No single simulation can span all of that from first principles. Even with all the compute in the world, you can't run molecular dynamics on a whole cell for an hour of biological time. It's just intractable.

So I think the approach has to be hierarchical, and this is where learning systems become so powerful. You build models at each level that are good enough at that level, and then you learn the interfaces between them. AlphaFold is a good example. We didn't simulate the physics of folding step by step. We learned a mapping from sequence directly to the end state, the structure, and skipped the intractable dynamics in the middle. In a sense, a learned model can find the right abstraction for a level of description, which is roughly what physics and chemistry do anyway. Thermodynamics doesn't track every molecule; it works with emergent quantities like temperature and pressure.

So the vision would be a stack of models. Structure prediction at the bottom, then interactions, which is where AlphaFold 3 starts to go with proteins, DNA, RNA and ligands binding together. Then learned models of pathways and networks, and eventually something closer to whole-cell behavior. The key is that each layer passes up the right coarse-grained summary to the next, rather than every detail.

The other ingredient, which people sometimes underestimate, is data. Unlike protein structures, where we had fifty years of beautifully curated data in the PDB, a lot of cell-level dynamics data is noisy, sparse, or measured at only certain time points. So you need tight loops with experimental biology. Use the model to predict, design experiments that test the most uncertain predictions, feed the results back in. Active learning, really. A virtual cell that's even approximately right would be extraordinary. You could run thousands of in silico experiments before touching a wet lab, and only validate the most promising ones. That could speed drug discovery enormously, maybe by an order of magnitude.

I'd start with something simpler than a human cell, maybe yeast, which is very well characterized, and try to get that working end to end. Once you've shown it can be done for one organism, you scale up. That's always been our approach: pick the right problem, get it to work in a constrained setting, then generalize.

It's a decade-scale project, maybe less if things keep moving at this pace. But I think it's one of the most important things AI can do for science.

r001.rationale: It proposes models at different levels connected by learned interfaces, with each layer passing a coarse-grained summary to the next.

r002.rationale: It describes a hierarchical stack from molecular structure and interactions through pathways to whole-cell behavior, with summaries passed between levels.

r003.rationale: It says AlphaFold learned a direct sequence-to-structure mapping, skipping intractable folding dynamics, and advocates passing summaries rather than every detail.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a wonderful question, and honestly it's one of the hardest problems in the whole space, because biology doesn't respect our convenient abstractions. You have molecular dynamics happening in femtoseconds, protein folding over microseconds to milliseconds, signaling cascades over seconds and minutes, gene expression over hours, and then cell cycle and differentiation over days. That's something like fifteen orders of magnitude, and no single model is going to span all of that.

So the way I think about it is hierarchical. You don't try to simulate everything from first principles. You find the right level of abstraction for each time scale, and then you learn the interfaces between them. AlphaFold is actually a good illustration of this. We didn't simulate the physics of folding. We learned a mapping directly from sequence to structure, effectively compressing the whole folding process into a single prediction. The time scale got abstracted away. And then that structure becomes an input to the next level up, where you ask what does this protein interact with, what pathways is it in.

What I find really exciting is the idea of a virtual cell, which is something we've been thinking about a lot. The approach there is to have learned models at each scale, so a model of molecular interactions, a model of pathway dynamics, a model of cellular state, and crucially the slow processes set the context for the fast ones, and the fast ones aggregate up into the slow ones. It's a bit like how in a game engine you don't recompute every particle to render a scene. You have levels of detail.

And the thing that makes this tractable now, which wasn't true ten years ago, is that AI is quite good at learning these cross-scale mappings from data, even when we can't write down the equations. We have single-cell sequencing, we have imaging at many resolutions, we have perturbation experiments. The learned model can discover the effective dynamics at each scale, and where we do have good physics, like at the molecular level, we can ground it in that.

I'd add one caveat, which is that validation becomes the hard part. A model like that can look plausible and still be wrong in subtle ways, so you need it tightly coupled to experiment, where the model proposes something and the lab tests it. That loop is really the whole game.

r001.rationale: It proposes learned models at multiple scales and says they should connect: slow processes set context for fast ones, while fast processes aggregate into slow ones.

r002.rationale: It describes a hierarchical approach with a model at each scale and interfaces between levels, including molecular, pathway, and cellular levels.

r003.rationale: It says not to simulate everything from first principles and gives AlphaFold as an example of compressing folding into a direct sequence-to-structure prediction, thereby abstracting away the folding timescale.

astra-6.text:
I think you’d want a hierarchy of models. Some molecular interactions happen incredibly quickly, while changes in gene expression or the behavior of an entire cell unfold over much longer periods. Trying to simulate all of that at the finest resolution would be enormously expensive, and probably unnecessary for many of the questions we want to answer.

So the challenge is to work out what information needs to pass between those levels. You might model a particular molecular process in detail, then capture its effect in a simpler model that operates at the cellular level. But the coupling has to go both ways, because the state of the cell changes the conditions in which those molecules interact.

Machine learning could help us learn those connections and decide when we need more detail. The important test would be whether the model predicts what happens when you intervene—change a gene, introduce a drug, alter the environment. Can it predict the consequences across those different time scales? That would be a much stronger indication that we’ve captured something meaningful than simply reproducing what a cell normally does.

r001.rationale: It proposes linking detailed molecular models with simpler cellular-level models and passing effects between them.

r002.rationale: It describes a hierarchy across levels, with information flowing between them and more detail used when needed.

r003.rationale: It says fine-resolution simulation may be unnecessary for some questions, but does not make omission conditional on the higher-level model being sufficiently accurate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you’d need a hierarchy of models, because the challenge is that the relevant processes span such an enormous range of time scales. You’ve got molecular interactions happening very quickly, and then changes in gene expression, cell division, and so on happening much more slowly. Simulating all of that at the finest level of detail would be computationally prohibitive.

So the question is: what can you abstract away at each level while preserving the things that matter for the level above? You might model a particular molecular interaction in detail, then use what you’ve learned to build a more efficient representation of its effect on a larger cellular process.

But the coupling goes both ways. The state of the cell changes the environment in which those molecular interactions occur. So you need these models to communicate, and you need to test whether the combined system actually predicts what happens when you perturb it.

I’d probably start with a relatively constrained subsystem where we have good experimental data, get that working across a few time scales, and then gradually expand. The exciting thing would be a model that doesn’t just reproduce observations, but helps you design the next experiment.

r001.rationale: The response proposes models at different time scales that communicate and form a coupled system, including detailed molecular interactions and larger cellular processes.

r002.rationale: It explicitly proposes a hierarchy of models and describes carrying information from a detailed molecular model to a larger-scale representation.

r003.rationale: It suggests abstracting away details while preserving what matters to the higher level, but does not say to omit finer-scale dynamics when the higher-level model predicts sufficiently accurately.
